---
title: Standing Rules
llms-description: "The _steward.md file: settings Steward enforces unattended above prose an agent applies, the rule that it may never say anything the definition could say, and how rules accumulate so a run gets quieter."
---

## Overview

`_steward.md` is where you say what you want, standing, for this project. It has
two halves in one file:

> **The front matter is what Steward executes at 3am with nobody watching. The
> prose is what an agent applies when it arrives.**

``` {.markdown filename="_steward.md"}
---
max_workers: 8
tend_interval: 10m
---

# _steward.md

## What is expected here

Sandbox startup times out on roughly 1% of samples in this eval; that is the
environment, not the model. Invalidate and re-run.

## Pre-authorised

Re-run samples that failed on provider rate limits, up to twice, without asking.
```

An empty file is a valid one: everything then escalates to you. `init` writes a
template whose front matter is entirely commented out, which parses as *no
preferences expressed* — deliberately, because a template shipping live values
would make Steward's defaults look like your decisions.

## Why one file rather than two

The obvious arrangement is two files — machine settings here, human guidance
there — and it is wrong, because that boundary is a fact about **Steward's
current capability rather than about your intent**, and it moves as Steward
improves.

Today `max_workers: 8` is executable and *"back off at the first sign of
throttling"* is prose an agent interprets. Next quarter the second may be
executable too. Splitting the file would make that seam visible to *you*, so
your mental model would have to track our implementation.

What adjacency buys is that you write one thought — *"never go past eight
workers here, and if the sonnet arm starts failing systematically, pause it and
tell me"* — and the executable half sits directly above the reasoning for it.
Neither can drift, and a reader arriving cold sees every standing instruction in
one place.

## Steward never writes this file

It proposes changes; you make them. A command that wanted to change a setting
prints the change to make rather than making it.

The reason is that an edit Steward made to your standing rules is, afterwards,
indistinguishable from one you made — and the whole value of the file is that
reading it tells you what a person decided. That costs one round trip and buys
an artifact nobody has to trust Steward about.

It applies to both halves. The front matter is more tempting because it is
machine-shaped, which is exactly why it needs saying.

## The front matter

Every key is a standing property of *this workspace and this host*. Values are
validated strictly and an unrecognised key is rejected outright, because this is
input being read before it changes what runs, not history being replayed.

| key | | |
|----|----|----|
| `max_tasks` | how many tasks may run at once, across the whole fleet | unbounded — every task starts immediately |
| `max_workers` | how many worker processes those are divided into | unbounded — a process per task |
| `stall_after` | consecutive fruitless attempts before a task stops being respawned | how much patience a project's failures deserve is genuinely a property of the project |
| `tend_interval` | how often a scheduled tend runs | **written with a unit** — `10m`, not `10` |

The file grows one key per feature rather than shipping a schema up front, since
a key that parses and does nothing is a lie about what the workspace controls.

::: {.callout-important}
### Durations need their unit

`tend_interval: 10` is refused. It is a perfectly good integer that means ten
minutes to whoever typed it and ten seconds to whoever wrote the parser, so
Steward will not guess.

The same strictness catches a subtler one. YAML reads `max_workers: yes` as
`True`, and a coercive validator would then read `True` as `1` — a workspace
that meant to say something ends up throttled to a single worker with nothing
reported. Validation is strict, and the error names the value that *arrived*, so
you can see what YAML did to what you typed.
:::

### `tend_interval` is a preference, not what is installed

Arming reads it, but a timer armed at one interval and a file later edited to
another disagree until somebody re-arms. That shows up as a `timer_drift` item
rather than something a turn quietly fixes — reaching into your crontab
unprompted is not a mechanical act. See [Reading Status](status.qmd).

## What may not go in it

> **The file may express only what your definition cannot.**

Your definition is the single source of truth for what an eval set *is*, and a
second file beside it is precisely where a contradicting `log_dir` or `model`
would end up. So keys the definition owns are **refused by name**, with a message
saying where they belong:

``` text
`max_samples` does not belong in _steward.md — set it in the definition
```

Refused this way: `log_dir`, `model`, `models`, `tasks`, `epochs`, `limit`,
`solver`, `scorer`, `sandbox`, `token_limit`, `time_limit`, `message_limit`,
`fail_on_error`, `retry_on_error`, and `max_samples`. Notification and store
settings are refused too, and point at their environment variables — a
notification URL is a credential, and keeping credentials out of files, shell
history, and process listings is a discipline Steward inherits and will not
break.

**The rule is sharper than "is it useful to Steward".** `max_samples` is the case
that teaches it: Steward genuinely needs the number, writes it into every worker,
and has a field for it — and it is still refused, because `eval_set(max_samples=…)`
can say it and a workspace-level constant would silently outrank an author who
did. `max_workers` passes in the other direction, because the fan-out into
processes is Steward's invention and no `eval_set()` argument reaches it.

Whether Steward *consumes* a value is not the question. Whether the definition
could express it is.

`max_tasks` is the case that shows the rule is about *scope* rather than about
spelling. `eval_set(max_tasks=…)` exists and means how many tasks one process
runs at once; the key here means how many run at once across a fleet of
processes, which is a thing no definition can see. They cannot contradict each
other, because Steward writes the per-process number into every worker itself —
so the definition's own `max_tasks` never reaches a worker to be overruled.

## When it cannot be read

A malformed file does not stop the run. The turn recovers the last settings a
previous turn recorded, proceeds on those, and reports a `degraded` item saying
so. Where the *reason* goes is `steward.log`, because a file Steward could not
parse is a fact about Steward.

With no prior turn to fall back on there is nothing to recover, and the command
refuses — defaults would silently discard what you wrote, which is the one
outcome worse than stopping.

The prose half is **never parsed**, so no amount of malformed writing below the
front matter can break a turn.

## The prose

There is no schema here. The template suggests headings because they are the
questions that come up, not because anything reads them:

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **What is expected here** | failures you already know about, so nobody wakes you for them |
| **What always reaches me** | the inverse — things you want to see even if they look routine |
| **Pre-authorised** | rulings granted in advance. An agent acting on one is executing a decision you already made |
| **Concurrency envelope** | the room an agent may move in beneath `max_tasks`, which takes judgement rather than a number |
| **Notes for whoever reads this next** | what this eval set is for, and what a third party picking up the directory cold would need in order to judge the results |

**Pre-authorisation is the one that pays best**, and it is worth understanding
why. A rule written only as prose fires only when an agent is in session —
precisely when it is least needed. A rule the front matter can express holds
overnight. As Steward's executable half grows, rules migrate upward across that
line; your intent does not change, only who can act on it.

## A ruling is not a policy

The distinction that keeps this file trustworthy:

-   A **ruling** is your decision about one situation, with all of that
    situation's context behind it.
-   A **policy** is a standing rule for every future situation of that shape.

Promoting the first into the second is itself a judgement, and it is yours.
Auto-promotion would quietly convert *"invalidate those 47 rate-limit errors
from the 15:40 outage"* into *"always invalidate rate-limit errors"* — a
different and much larger claim, which you never made. For a tool whose output
is evaluation results, silently widening your standards is close to the worst
failure available.

So rulings land in the journal automatically, and promotion into `_steward.md`
is proposed and never assumed. Over months your actual standards accumulate in
place of the ones you guessed at up front, which gives the whole workflow a
legible success metric: **interruptions per run, trending down.**
